FOREWORD 


This Indian Standard [P : 22] (Third Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards after the draft 
finalized by the Methods of Sampling and Test for Petroleum, its Products, Gaseous Fuels and Lubricants Sectional 
Committee and approval of the Petroleum, Coal and Related Products Division Council. 


This Indian standard was revised for second time in 1985 based on IP/143/82. In this revision, considerable 
assistance was derived from IP 143/2004 ‘Determination of asphaltenes (heptane insolubles) in crude petroleum 
and petroleum products’ and ISO 12185 ‘Crude petroleum and petroleum products — Determination of 
density — Oscillating U-tube method’. Amendment no. 1 issued in 1995 has also been included. In the present 
revision, details of distillation apparatus was removed and IS 1448 [P : 18] has been referred to, in its place. 
Additionally, a method for determination of density is included, in line with international practices. 


In reporting the results of a test or analysis made in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or 
calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS 2 : 1960 ‘Rules for rounding off numerical 
values (revised)’. 


IS 1448 [P : 22] : 2019 


Indian Standard 


METHODS OF TEST FOR 
PETROLEUM AND ITS PRODUCTS 


[P : 22] 
DETERMINATION OF ASPHALTENES (HEPTANE INSOLUBLES) 
IN CRUDE PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS 


( Third Revision ) 


1 SCOPE 


1.1 This standard [P : 22] describes the procedure for 
determination of the heptane insoluble asphaltenes 
content present in gas oil, diesel fuel, residual fuel oils, 
lubricating oils, bitumen and crude petroleum which 
has been topped to an oil temperature of 260°C (see 
Annex A). 


1.2 The precision is applicable to values between 0.5 
and 30.0 percent m/m. The values outside this range 
may still be valid, but may not give the same precision 
values. Presence of additives in the oils may lead to 
imprecise results. 


WARNING — This use of this standard may involve 
hazardous materials, operation and equipment. This 
standard does not purport to address all of the safety 
problems associated with its use. It is the responsibility 
of the user of this standard to establish appropriate safety 
and health practices and determine the applicability of 
regulatory limitations prior to use. 


2 REFERENCES 


The following standards contain provisions, which, 
through reference in this text, constitute provisions of 
this standard. At the time of publication, the editions 
indicated were valid. All standards are subject to 
revision, and parties to agreements based on this 
standard are encouraged to investigate the possibility 
of applying the most recent editions of the standards 
indicated below:

3 TERMINOLOGY 


For the purpose of this test, the following definition 
shall apply. 


3.1 Asphaltenes — Represent an oil fraction that is 
soluble in a specified aromatic solvent, such as toluene), 
but separates up on addition of an excess paraffinic 
solvent, such as heptane. 
NOTE — Asphaltenes are the organic molecules of high 
molecular weight, occurring in crude petroleum and 
petroleum products. Their composition normally includes a 


disproportionately high concentration of sulphur, nitrogen and 
metals. 


3.2 Crude petroleum Residue — Residue from 
distillation to an oil temperature of 260°C carried 
out under the conditions of the specific preparatory 
procedure mentioned in Annex A. 


4 OUTLINE OF THE METHOD 


4.1 A test sample is mixed with heptane and is heated 
under reflux. The precipitated asphaltenes, waxy 
substances and inorganic material are gathered on a 
filter paper. The waxy substances are expelled in an 
extractor by washing with hot heptane. 


4.2 After removal of the waxy substances, the 
asphaltenes are isolated from the inorganic material 
by dissolution in hot toluene. The extraction solvent is 
evaporated, and the asphaltenes are weighed. 


5 APPARATUS 


5.1 Ground-glass, joints from different sources may 
have one of two diameter to length ratios. For the 
purposes of this standard, either is suitable, and for few 
applications, the diameter itself can be one of two. In 


IS 1448 [P : 22] : 2019 


any case, it is critical that the male and female parts of 
each joint are from the same series to avoid recession 
or protuberance. 


5.2 Condenser, with a coil or double surface, fitted 
with a 34/45 or 34/35 ground-glass joint at the bottom 
to fit the top of the extractor. Minimum length 300 mm. 


5.3 Reflux Extractor, conforming to the dimensions 
given in Fig 1. Tolerances are +1 mm on the height and 
outer diameter (OD) of the extractor body, and + 0.5 
mm on all other dimensions. The female ground-glass 
joint at the top shall match the male at the bottom! of 
the condenser, and the male ground-glass joint at the 
bottom shall match the female of the conical flask. 


All dimensions in millimetres. 


Fic. 1 EXTRACTOR 


5.4 Conical Flasks, of borosilicate glass of appropriate 
capacity (see 9.2 and Table 1), with ground-glass joints 
to fit the bottom of the extractor. 


NOTE — Sizes 24/39, 24/29, 29/43 or 29/32 are suitable. 


5.5 Stopper, borosilicate glass, to fit the conical flask. 


5.6 Evaporating Vessel, borosilicate glass. Either a 
hemispherical dish of 90 + 5 mm diameter, or another 
suitable vessel used in conjunction with a rotovapor. 


NOTE — A rotovapor in conjunction with a nitrogen 
atmosphere reduces the hazard of toluene evaporation (see 9.7) 


5.7 Filter Funnel, borosilicate glass, 100 + 5 mm 
diameter. 


5.8 Filter Papers, Whatman grade 42, 110 or 125 mm 
diameter. 


5.9 Analytical Balance, accuracy of 0.1 mg. 


5.10 Forceps, stainless steel, spade ended. 


5.11 Timing Device, electronic or manual, accurate 
to 1.0s. 


5.12 Oven, 100 to 110°C. 
5.13 Graduated Cylinders, 50 ml and 100 ml capacity. 


5.14 Stirring Rods, glass or polytetrafluorethylene 
(PTFE), 150 x 3 mm diameter. 


5.15 Cooling Vessel, consisting of either a desiccators 
without desiccant, or another suitable tightly stoppered 
vessel. 


5.16 Mixer, high-speed, non-aerating. 
6 REAGENTS 


6.1 Toluene (Methylbenzene) [C,H.CH,] — Analytical 
reagent or nitration grade. 


6.2 Heptane [C_H,,] — Analytical reagent grade. 
7 SAMPLE PREPARATION 


7.1 Test portions from the laboratory samples shall be 
drawn after thorough mixing and subdivision. Heat 
viscous samples of residual fuels to a temperature, 
which renders the sample liquid, but not above 
80°C, and homogenize using the mixer (see 5.16), as 
necessary. 


7.2 Heat samples of penetration grade bitumen to a 
temperature not exceeding 120°C, and stir well before 
taking an aliquot. 


7.3 Samples of hard bitumen shall be ground to a 
powder before an aliquot is taken. 


7.4 Samples of crude petroleum shall be prepared as 
mentioned in Annex A, unless it is known that the crude 
petroleum contains negligible quantities of material 
with boiling point below 80°C. 


8 APPARATUS PREPARATION 


8.1 Clean all glass apparatus, by using a strongly 
oxidizing agent, such as ammonium peroxydisulphate 
in concentrated sulphuric acid at approximately 8 g/l, 
or sulphuric acid itself. Immerse for at least 12 h. Rinse 
with tap water, followed by distilled water and then by 
acetone. 


8.2 For routine analysis, use a proprietary laboratory 
detergent to clean the glassware, followed by the rinses 
described in 8.1. When the detergent cleaning does not 
match the cleanliness required (visual appearance), use 
a strong oxidizing agent. 


8.3 After rinsing, place the glassware in the oven 
(see 5.12) for 30 min, and cool in the cooling vessel 
(see 5.15) for 30 min before weighing. 


9 PROCEDURE 


9.1 Estimate the asphaltene content of the sample, or 
residue obtained from the procedure in Annex A, and 
weigh the quantity, to the nearest 1 mg for masses 
above | g, and to the nearest 0.1 mg for masses of | g 
and below, indicated in Table | into a flask (see 5.4). 


9.2 Add heptane (see 6.2) to the test portion in the flask 
at a ratio of 30 ml to each 1 g of sample if the expected 
asphaltene content is below 25 percent (m/m). For 
samples with an expected asphaltene content of above 
25 percent (m/m), a minimum heptane volume of 25 ml 
shall be used.

Heptane Volume

9.3 Mix the contents until the test portion has fully 
dispersed within the heptane, then boil the mixture 
under reflux for 60 + 5 min. Remove the flask and 
contents at the end of this period, cool, close with a 
stopper (see 5.5), and store in a dark cupboard for 90 
to 150 min. 


9.4 Place the filter paper, folded as shown in Fig. 2 
(so as to prevent loss of asphaltenes by creeping), in the 
filter funnel using forceps. Handle the filter paper with 
forceps only. Without agitation, decant the liquid into 
the filter paper. Then transfer the residue in the flask 
as completely as possible with successive quantities 
of hot heptane, using the stirring rod (see 5.14), if 
necessary. Give the flask a final rinse with hot heptane 
and pour the rinsings through the filter. Set the flask 
aside for further use, without washing, as prescribed 
in 9.6. 


9.5 Remove the filter paper and contents from the 
funnel and place in the reflux extractor (see 5.3). Using 
a flask different from that used initially, reflux with 
heptane (see 6.2) at a rate of 2 to 4 drops/s from the 
end of the condenser for an extraction period of not 
less than 1 h, or until a few drops of heptane from the 


IS 1448 [P : 22] : 2019 


bottom of the extractor leave no residue on evaporation 
on a glass slide. 


APER CLIP 


Fic. 2 FILTER PAPER 


9.6 Replace the flask by the one used initially, and to 
which has been added 30 to 60 ml of toluene (6.1), and 
continue refluxing until all the asphaltenes have been 
dissolved from the paper. 


9.7 Transfer the contents of the flask to a clean and dry 
evaporating vessel (see 5.6), weighed to the nearest 0.2 
mg by tare against a similar dish. Wash out the flask 
with successive small quantities of toluene to a total not 
exceeding 30 ml. Remove the toluene by evaporation 
on a boiling water bath or by evaporation in a rotovapor 
under an atmosphere of nitrogen. 


CAUTION — Perform the evaporation in a fume 
cupboard. 


9.8 Dry the dish and contents in the oven (see 5.12) at 
approximately 100°C for 30 min. Cool in the cooling 
vessel (see 5.15) for 30 to 60 min and re-weigh by 
tare against the dish used previously for this purpose, 
and which has been subjected to the same heating 
and cooling procedure as was the dish containing 
asphaltenes. 

NOTE — Asphaltenes are very susceptible to oxidation, and 


it is important that the procedure specified in the final drying 
stage is adhered. 


10 CALCULATION 


10.1 Calculate the asphaltene content, A, in percent 
(m/m), of the petroleum product using the equation: 


Ati 
G 


Where, 
M= is the mass of asphaltenes, in grams; and 
G= is the mass of the test portion, in grams. 


IS 1448 [P : 22] : 2019 


10.2 Calculate the asphaltene content, C, in percent 
(m/m), of crude petroleum prepared in the manner 
described in Annex A, using the equation: 


C=100x E ® 
(Gx D) 
Where, 
= is the mass of asphaltenes, in grams; 
= is the mass of residue from the distillation, in 
grams; 
G= is the mass of the residue aliquot, in grams’ 
and 
D= is the mass of the crude petroleum sample 


distilled, in grams. 


11 EXPRESSION OF RESULTS 


11.1 Report the heptane insoluble asphaltene content 
of values less than 1.00 percent (m/m), to the nearest 
0.05 percent (m/m). 


11.2 Report the heptane insoluble asphaltene content of 
values of 1.0 percent (m/m) and greater, to the nearest 
0.1 percent (m/m). 


12 PRECISION 


12.1 Repeatability, r 


The difference between two successive test results 
obtained by the same operator with the same apparatus 
under constant operating conditions on identical test 
material would, in the normal and correct operation of 
the test method should not exceed the value below: 


r=0.1A 


where, 


A= is the average result, in percent (m/m). 


12.2 Reproducibility, R 


The difference between two single and independent 
results obtained by different operators working in 
different laboratories on nominally identical test 
material would, in the normal and correct operation 
of the test method, should not exceed the value 
below: 


R=02A 
Where, 


A= is the average result, in percent (m/m). 


13 BIAS 


Since heptane insoluble asphaltenes are defined by 
this procedure, no bias can be assigned. The term 
‘asphaltenes’ may be associated with other similar 
procedures using alkanes as precipitating agents other 
than heptane. In general, lighter alkanes will give 
higher results, and heavier alkanes will give lower 
results than heptane, but no consistent ratio can be 
assigned. 


14 TEST REPORT 
The test report shall contain at least the following 
information: 

a) areference to this standard; 


b) all details necessary for complete identification of 
the product tested; 


c) the result of the test (see 11); 


d) any deviation, by agreement or otherwise, from 
the procedure specified; and 


e) the date of the test. 


IS 1448 [P : 22] : 2019 


ANNEX A 
( Clauses 1.1, 3.2, 7.4, 9.1 and 10.2 ) 


PREPARATION OF CRUDE PETROLEUM RESIDUE BY DISTILLATION 


A-1 SCOPE 


This annex describes a procedure for the preparation of 
a crude petroleum residue (topped to an oil temperature 
of 260 °C) suitable for the determination of asphaltene 
content (see 9.1). 


A-2 PRINCIPLE 


A weighed test portion of the crude petroleum sample 
is distilled in specified glass apparatus under specified 
conditions of heat input and rate of distillation. The 
distillation is stopped at an oil temperature of 260°C 
and the mass of the residue determined. 


A-3 APPARATUS 


A-3.1 Distillation Apparatus 


The apparatus shall conform to the requirements of 
IS 1448 [P : 18], with the exception of the temperature 
sensor. The temperature sensor shall be a liquid-in-glass 
thermometer of total immersion type of total length 300 
to 320 mm, with a temperature range of -4 to 360°C, 
and a maximum scale error of 2°C, or an alternative 
temperature measurement device or system of at least 
equivalent accuracy. A transparent bath, maintained at 
15 + 3°C, shall be used as receiver. 


NOTE — A suitable thermometer is an IP 4C. 


A-3.2 Drying Apparatus 


The drying apparatus shall consist of one of the 
following. 


A-3.2.1 Centrifuge 


A-3.2.2 Filter Apparatus — Operating at increased 
pressure. 


A-3.2.3 Steel Container — Capable of withstanding 
1000 kPa pressure, and of being heated to 200°C. 


A-3.2.4 Cottrell Type Electrostatic Separator 
A-4 SAMPLE PREPARATION 


A-4.1 If the crude petroleum contains sufficient water 
to cause difficulties in distillation (excessive foaming), 
dry the sample by a method that avoids the loss of 
volatile components. 


A-4.1.1 Separate the water by gravity or by centrifuging 
in a closed container at lowest practicable temperature. 


A-4.1.2 Filter the sample at the lowest practicable 
temperature and applied pressure, through anhydrous 


calcium chloride, sodium sulphate, or other suitable 
drying agent in a closed vessel. 


A-4.1.3 Heat the sample in a closed steel container 
(see A.3.2.3) fitted with a temperature sensor and 
pressure sensor. Fill the container to approximately 
70 percent capacity and heat it until the oil reaches 
a temperature of 200°C, or until the pressure reaches 
700 kPa. Allow the container to cool to ambient 
temperature and then decant the oil from the separated 
water. 


A-4.1.4 Separate the water electrostatically by 
an adaption of the Cottrell principle. A suitable 
apparatus consists of a tall glass beaker with a brass 
gauze cylinder fitting tightly inside and lined with 
flannel, which has been saturated with water and 
then squeezed out to leave it damp. The central 
electrode is of stirrer rotated about 30 rev/min. Pour 
the sample into the beaker and apply a voltage to 
the electrodes. Interrupt the water precipitation at 
intervals to prevent the loss of volatile components 
and allow the oil to cool. Separate the oil from the 
water that has coalesced and run down the flannel 
lining. 


A-4.1.5 Distil off the water with the more volatile 
components in the apparatus described in A-3.2. 
Charge the flask with 300 ml of sample, and place the 
temperature sensor such that the sensing point (bulb) is 
immersed in the sample. Heat the flask gently so that 
the oil temperature rises slowly to 150°C, vapourizing 
into the condenser by means of a small gas flame any 
drops of water that collect on the walls of the flask. 
Stop the distillation when no more water passes 
over in the distillate. Allow the residue to cool to 
room temperature. Run off the water collected in the 
separating funnel, and return the oily distillate to the 
residue and mix it thoroughly. If water is still visible, 
filter by the method described in A-4.1.2. 


A-5 PROCEDURE 


A-5.1 Determine the density at 15°C of the crude 
petroleum by IS1448 [P : 16] or IS 1448 [P : 167]/ 
ISO 12185. 


A-5.2 Weigh the distillation flask to the nearest 0.1 g 
and charge it with a mass equivalent to 100 ml of 
sample at 15°C to within 0.1 g. Ensure that no oil flows 
down the vapor tube during this operation. Record the 
mass of oil (D). Place the liquid-in-glass thermometer 
so that the bottom of the bulb is 2.0 + 0.5 mm from 
the bottom of the flask, or the alternative temperature 


IS 1448 [P : 22] : 2019 


sensor to a position established to give identical 
temperature readings. 


A-5.3 Swab out the condenser tube to remove any 
material remaining from a previous test. Place the flask 
and its contents in position with the vapor tube inserted 
into the condenser tube. Make this connection tight by 
means of a stopper or bung through which the vapor 
tube passes, and adjust the position of the flask so that 
vapour tube extends into the condenser tube not less 
than 25 mm and not more than 50 mm. 


A-5.4 Place a clean dry receiver at the outlet of the 
condenser, such that the condenser tube or adaptor 
extends into it at least 25 mm, but not below the 100 
ml mark. Immerse the receiver up to the 100 ml mark 
in the transparent bath. Cover the top of the receiver 
closely during the distillation with a piece of paper 


weighted to restrict volatile losses, and to overcome the 
buoyancy of the receiver in the water bath. Circulate 
ice cold (below 4°C) water through the condenser. 


A-5.5 Apply heat to the flask and distil the crude 
petroleum at a rate not exceeding 2.5 ml/min until it 
ceases to foam, after which keep the rate of distillation 
constant at 2.0 ml/min to 2.5 ml/min (approximately 
1 drop/s). Continue the distillation without interruption 
to 260°C. Stop the heating flask and allow the condenser 
to drain into the receiver. 


A-5.6 Allow the residue in the flask to cool, remove 
the temperature sensor, and weigh the flask and residue. 
Record the mass of the residue (R). 


A-5.7 Use this residue to carry out the procedure 
(see 9) for the determination of asphaltene content.
